en: Śrī:
The Nyāyakalāpasaṅgraha composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.

Having prostrated before Rāmānuja, the Lord of those who have attained self-restraint and the cause of awakening for the lotus of my heart, I compose this compendium of the principles of the Śārīraka [Brahma-sūtras], which brings within the range of vision the path to his realization. (1)

The nature of valid cognition, the refutation of its opposites, the means of attaining it, and the enjoyment of its fruit—these have been thoroughly examined here in this treatise by means of four chapters. (2)

At the outset, a collection of statements regarding the individual soul (jīva) and primordial matter (pradhāna) has been considered, which are respectively very indistinct, indistinct, distinct, and following the shadow [of the subject]. (3)
There is no contradiction with scripture or logic, and there is the refutation of opposing views;
for the ether and so forth, as well as the sense organs and so forth, possess the nature of being effects due to their being [enumerated] second in the list.

The state of being with defects and the state of being without defects of both the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para), as well as the worship of the Supreme and the prescribed duties, are all treated in the third [chapter]. (5)
The method for the practice of worship, the commencement of the journey,
the manner of the path of travel, and the fruit— these are presented in the fourth [chapter].

The first quarter [of the verse] has refuted the claim that the capacity for words to convey meaning is established through the linguistic usage of elders only in the case of what is to be accomplished (*kārya*), and not in the case of what is already established (*siddha*); for this capacity is well-known even regarding established entities when used to instruct the ignorant. (7)

Because there is no experience of a distinction [between them], the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or the indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) [of Brahman] would result in the impossibility of establishing [Brahman's] origin and so forth;
thus, the negation of both is also possible because of their shared incapacity [to define it]. (8)

By refuting the argument that "because it is an effect and possesses parts, its creator and cause are established," he has cast this aside by supporting the fact that [the Lord] is accessible through the scriptures alone. || 9 ||
"Since no purpose whatsoever is found in Brahman—which is eternally established—neither engagement nor cessation [is possible];
having thus raised the doubt regarding its lack of authoritativeness, [the author] has refuted it by showing that the Supreme Person is Himself the fruit. (10)

Having raised the doubt that [the Veda] is not a valid means of knowledge (*amāna*) due to the absence of etymological derivation, the difficulty of comprehension, its establishment by other means, and its fruitlessness, he refuted it by establishing each point through four logical arguments.
But the secondary [view] holds that "seeing" (īkṣā) refers to the Pradhāna because of its association with secondary seeing, since it is the cause of the worlds;
however, he rejected this as the primary [meaning], because the word "Self" (ātman) implies that the seeing is primary.
Fearing that the suffix *mayaṭ* here denotes a modification (*vikāra*), one might suspect that the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) is "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*).

[The author] refuted this by stating that it denotes abundance (*prācurya*), because [modification] is impossible [in the case of Brahman] and because [such a view] would result in the abandonment [of the primary sense] even in the case of "consisting of breath" (*prāṇamaya*). || 13 ||

Thinking that "only some conscious being, superior in merit, must occupy the center of the mandala," he thus dispelled their doubt by means of the attributes of the Supreme Self, such as being the Lord of the World.
He might indeed be designated by the specific name "Space," for he is the source of the worlds; or else, by signs such as the dissolution of beings, he was identified as "Prāṇa. || 15 ||
For it cannot be suspected that the characteristics of another's marks apply to one's own statement; for the Jyotis is indeed the third [foot] consisting of those elements.
This is not to be doubted, for the elements are not a foot of that [Jyotis], but rather of this Supreme Person. (16)
But as for Indra, since his status as the individual soul (jīva) has been determined, he might be the cause [of the world] based on the word regarding his own worship;
this, however, is not correct, for such instruction and the attribute of immortality belong to him only from the perspective of the scriptural vision (śāstradṛṣṭi). || 17 ||
With his former foot, he proclaimed the Self— the cause of the world, the source of life, radiant, possessing form, consisting of bliss, and endowed with consciousness— as his excellent abode.

In this scripture, however, he composed the remaining three chapters in order to clarify this very point: that Brahman alone is the direct cause of the worlds, possessing both consciousness and unconsciousness as its body. (19)

In that regard, by the second [reason] the body was established; by the third, the entire expansion of the sentient and insentient (cid-acit-prapañca) as being of the nature of that [body]; and by the fourth, its refutation as being otherwise than that. || 20 ||

Having raised every possible objection—on account of its being produced by its own karma, its status as a causal agent, its minuteness, and its having a limited abode—he refuted [the view that] the individual soul (jīva) [is the agent], based on its well-known nature, its qualities, and traditional scripture. (21)

But the claim that the self is the soul, not something else, being independent and the very one who experiences the fruits of karma—this too is incorrect; for that [self] is merely the consumption [of food] through the sprinkling of death upon all that moves and is stationary. || 22 ||

The claim that this [light] within the eye is the individual soul (jīva), or the reflected image, or even the divine (daiva), is likewise incorrect, because of the mention of immortality, the hearing of bliss, and because of the absence of instability. (23)

Because of the word "seer" (draṣṭṛ) here in the remainder of the sentence, and because of the negation of another seer, it is said that [the Self] is the Knower of the Field who controls the inner controller; this does not refer to the waking state, because of the mention of immortality (amṛtatva).
By the negation of grossness and visibility, the Pradhāna—subtle and characterized by invisibility—is [implied];
thus, the proposition that the Kṣetrajña alone is the Imperishable (Akṣara) would be incorrect, because it is higher than that which is beyond [the Pradhāna]. || 25 ||

"Is Vaiśvānara the fire in the stomach, or a deity, or perhaps a third entity denoted by the word 'fire'? It cannot be so, because [Vaiśvānara] has the three worlds as his body and is designated as the Puruṣa. (26)

Having first established the state of that body by means of its gross and subtle aspects, as well as its individual sense organs and its constituent parts, he subsequently refuted the notion that it was anything other than a body.

In this [verse], by means of this word "foot" (pāda), it is established—through both grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) and its opposite—that the world has that [Brahman] as its body. || 28 ||
The third quarter [of the verse] states:
Because it is the support of the senses beginning with the mind, the one who has heaven and earth as his support is indeed the conscious Self and none other.
This should not be doubted, because of the explicit use of the word "Self" (ātman) and because of the designation of Him as that which is to be approached by the liberated. 29.
The instruction, beginning with Name and so forth, was concluded with the individual soul (jīva) called Prāṇa;
therefore, one should not suspect that [the teaching] ends there, for the instruction on the True (Satya) is superior to this. || 30 ||
If it is argued that the Imperishable (akṣara) must be either the indeterminate (avyākṛta), or consciousness alone, or the substratum of space—
on the grounds that it is the locus of effects and the locus of insentient matter— that too is incorrect, because its support [is the Lord] and because it is governed by Him.
The world of Brahmā (brahmaloka), which is taught as being superior to the intermediate space (antarikṣa) [the Bhuva-loka], is the world of the Creator (vidhātṛloka).

Therein, it would be incorrect to say that "the Creator" is to be meditated upon through the *praṇava* consisting of three measures (*trimātra*), because of [his] designations such as "Immortal" (*amṛta*). || 32 ||
The ether (ākāśa) might indeed be the subtle body (dahara), or else the conscious self (cetana), on account of its well-known association [with space] and its connection with qualities;
yet this is not correct, for there is no reality in the ether, nor are desires naturally established in the individual soul (jīva). || 33 ||

In the statement, "The lord of life moves about," the claim that the individual soul (jīva) is measured by the size of a thumb based on common usage would likewise be incorrect, because in this very sentence the word "Īśāna" (the Lord) is heard.
"It is said that the gods, being bodiless, are not authorized to perform propitiation when one must accomplish [a rite] through a physical form;
but this too is false, for they possess imagined names and forms, and therefore they are as capable as humans. (35)

The Vasus and others do not possess eligibility for the Madhu-vidyā and similar meditations because they have already attained the status of Vasu; nor is it due to their being the objects of worship themselves, for there is no further desire [for them], since the Supreme alone is the object of worship. || 36 ||

It is not true that even those devoid of Vedic study, having heard the *Mahābhārata* and other texts and thereby realized the Supreme Person, worship Him; for there is a prohibition against such Śūdras hearing [the Vedas] and so forth. (37)
In the statement "having shaken off," that which was previously under discussion—the liberated one alone—attains the state of space.
For this [liberated one] does not breathe, nor do name and form sustain him; indeed, neither the bound nor the liberated [in this sense] are such [as to require sustenance]. 38.

In this [text], it has been demonstrated that [the Self] possesses an unafflicted nature, the form of bliss, the quality of being a ruler, the quality of being a refuge, the excellence of its attributes, the state of being beyond reproach, and the quality of being the sustainer. (39)
In the third [chapter], the identity of the individual and collective forms of both Pradhāna and Jīva is stated in sequence, and furthermore, their status as the governing authority is also declared.

But by means of the fourth and fifth [sūtras], its nature as the Self is established both in its own form and through its attributes for the purpose of being meditated upon; such is the purpose of [establishing] its nature as the Self. (41)

"Even though he is not the lord with respect to those various relations, he feels aversion"—according to this maxim, the sixth [chapter] was taught for the sake of establishing the nature of the Self. (42)
In the middle [section], as a consequence of the discussion regarding the specific distinctions of the sixth [chapter] and the God of gods,
the eligibility of Śūdras for the Vidyā and the absence thereof have been established.
But from the seventh [verse] onwards, lordship is established by virtue of being the sustainer. || 43 ||
Thus, by these three quarters, Brahman has been established as the cause;
by the fourth, it is further demonstrated that causality belongs to Him alone. (44)
The fourth quarter:

"The unmanifest is beyond the Great; the Person is beyond that; there is nothing higher than that"—this enumeration of established categories and their systematic arrangement is not correct here. For, among those things mentioned as being like the chariot-parts, such as speech and the rest, the "unmanifest" is simply the body, and the "Person" is this very Supreme Puruṣa. || 45 ||
In this statement, "the Unborn," that which is not explicitly stated is the Pradhāna, because of its independence and its role in effecting the creation of the entire world.

Indeed, in this context, only the act of creating is mentioned, as there is no specific [qualification]; however, the Śruti speaks of a specific [entity], and therefore [it refers to Brahman]. || 46 ||
In the statement, "In which [abode] there are the five peoples, the five, and also the sky," because the number is clearly included, this counting according to the Tantras does not indeed hold.

Because they abide as supports for Brahman, because their manifestation is preeminent, and because they function as designations, the pentad of the senses beginning with breath (prāṇa) is likewise [counted]; thus, as in the case of "seven" for the seven sages (saptarṣayaḥ). || 47 ||

Because of the various statements of causal doctrines—such as "in some places it is existent," "in some places it is the Self," "in some places it is non-existent," "in some places it is the Puruṣa," and "in some places it is Brahman"—there is indeed no definitive conclusion anywhere; for in every case, the Supreme is drawn toward [the truth] by means of indicative marks, context, secondary qualities, and so forth. (48)

"One who is the agent of whatever action"—the person thus mentioned here is indeed the individual soul (*jīva*), because he possesses agency and possession of action, and because his state as an enjoyer is perceived through his innate, inherent qualities. Such a doubt should not be raised; for in this statement, the world is what is denoted by the word "action. The mention of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the individual soul (*jīva*) here is for the sake of illustration, since Brahman is the substratum of deep sleep. || 49 ||

In this passage concerning the statement that the dearness of the husband and others is produced by oneself, the individual soul (jīva) is the subject to be understood; for it is heard here that the relationship with husband, wife, and so forth is to be seen [by him].

Indeed, the syntactical connection of the sentence does not apply to anything else, nor is the state of being the cause of immortality stated [of another]; furthermore, at the end of the sentence, there is the hearing of a characteristic mark of the individual soul, which exists within the Supreme due to its location.

If the other [the effect] were different from the material cause (*upādāna*), there would be no synthesis in a single locus; furthermore, the scriptural teaching regarding the absence of modification (*avikāritva*) remains awake in the world.

Therefore, it cannot be said that the Supreme is not the material cause, because of the initial proposition, because both [cause and effect] are explicitly stated, and because of the inquiry, "What could it be? (KU 3.1). || 51 ||
Because of their processes, their recognitions, their descriptions of intrinsic natures, and likewise because of their inclusion of numbers, they are mutually inconsistent with one another. (52)

Because of the mention of the connection with karma, because of the hearing of [terms such as] "husband" and so forth, and because a distinction between the material cause and the efficient cause is observed in the world. (53)
"The cause is Brahman alone and nothing else"—this is not at all a certainty;
thus, what was stated by the Tantrikas has been refuted by this [verse]. 54.
By three [reasons] there would be the refutation of Primordial Matter (pradhāna); by the fourth, the resolution of mutual contradictions;
and by the fifth and sixth, the individual soul (jīva) is turned away from both liberation and bondage. (55)
By this much of the collection of aphorisms, he refuted the atheistic Sāṃkhya; from the remainder, he shook off the [theistic] Sāṃkhya who desired the identity of the efficient cause and God. (56)

Thus, by all the statements of those who propound the cause of the world, speaking with one voice, it is established that Brahman alone—the omniscient and possessed of infinite power—is the source of these worlds. (57)

That Supreme Brahman, having a subtle body composed of consciousness and unconscious matter, becomes the cause; and again, having a gross body composed of consciousness and unconscious matter, it becomes the effect. (58)
The first quarter [of this work] establishes that, due to its contradiction with Smṛti, the Upabṛṃhaṇa (the Purāṇas) cannot be the source for the world originating from Brahman;
this [objection] is without substance because it contradicts other Smṛtis, and the possibility of those [other Smṛtis] being unauthoritative cannot even be suspected.
The meaning established by the Vedānta as "Brahman" is not correct, because it lacks support from the Smṛti regarding the Lord;
this is not so, because of contradictions with other [scriptures] and because the possibility of delusion exists due to [the Lord being conceived as] a living soul (jīva). || 2 ||

Whatever is an effect does not possess the same qualities as its cause; this Brahman and this universe are likewise distinct. If it is argued that [Brahman] possesses attributes such as knowledge and ignorance, or that consciousness arises from the act of seeing, [we reply: yadi kāraṇadharmāṇāṃ kārye 'nugama iṣyate | tarhi sarvajñatādīnāṃ brahmaṇo 'pi bhavedasau || 4 || If the persistence of the causal attributes in the effect is desired, then omniscience and other such qualities would also belong to Brahman. atha kāryasya dharmāṇāṃ kāraṇe 'nanvayo mataḥ | tarhi sarvajñatādīnāṃ brahmaṇo 'pi nivartanam || 5 || Alternatively, if it is held that the attributes of the effect do not persist in the cause, then omniscience and other such qualities would be excluded from Brahman as well. tasmāt kāryakāraṇayor bhedo 'vaśyam abhīpsitavyaḥ | anyathā sarvajñatvājñatvādivirodho duṣpariharaḥ || 6 || Therefore, a distinction between cause and effect must necessarily be accepted; otherwise, the contradiction between omniscience and ignorance would be difficult to resolve. nanu māyopahitaṃ brahma jagatkāraṇam ucyate | māyā ca tadguṇair yuktaiva tasmād doṣa eva na || 7 || [Objection: It is said that Brahman, conditioned by Māyā, is the cause of the world; and since Māyā is indeed endowed with its own qualities, there is no fault. maivam | māyāyā api brahmavivartatvena taddharmāṇām api brahmaṇy ananvayāt | na hi rajjvāḥ sarpabhāve rajjudharmāḥ sarpe 'nugacchanti || 8 || Not so; for since Māyā too is an illusory transformation (vivarta) of Brahman, its attributes likewise do not persist in Brahman. Indeed, when a rope appears as a snake, the attributes of the rope do not follow into the snake. tasmād ekasyaiva brahmaṇaḥ sarvajñatvājñatvādiviruddhadharmāśrayatvaṃ nopapadyate | ato jagadbrahmaṇor atyantabhedo 'bhyupagantavyaḥ || 9 || Therefore, it is not tenable for the one Brahman alone to be the locus of contradictory attributes such as omniscience and ignorance. Consequently, an absolute difference between the world and Brahman must be admitted.
However, it does not appear reasonable to say that [the soul] is the very same as those deities;
for if there were no distinction in substance between the fly and so forth and the worm and so forth, then the relationship between cause and effect would be undermined. (4)

It might be argued that Brahman would possess the state of being an enjoyer, like the individual soul (jīva), because of its having a body; therefore, nothing more than this [limited self] would be established as Brahman.

This doubt should not be raised, for [the objection does not apply] because of the abandonment of karma, as in the case of one who is liberated; and this is also appropriate in the world, as in the case of a king. || 5 ||

If one were to argue that the identity of the cause and the effect cannot be established through distinctions such as mental forms (*buddhyākāra*), designations (*abhidhāna*), conventional usage (*vyavahṛti*), and enumeration (*gaṇanā*), this would not be sound; furthermore, there would be the consequence of the causal factors (*kāraka*) being purposeless.

However, since [the entity] denoted by terms such as "Being" (*sat*), "Brahman," and "Self" (*ātman*) is non-different from the word itself, and since the distinction between words and so forth depends upon the states of the substance, the consequence of the causal factors being purposeless does not arise here.

Since the statement "That thou art" and others declare the identity of the individual soul with Brahman, no one who desires his own happiness would indeed create a world that is the sole root of suffering.

Nor is this [identity] negated by such statements as "One of these two is different," for even the scriptural hearing of distinctions such as the body being the self serves the purpose of teaching the unity of consciousness. (7)
For that which is dependent on an agent and the object of service would be the supreme Brahman, but it is not dependent on anything else;
therefore, you cannot say "it is not the cause," because milk does not itself desire to become curd.

Brahman would have to be an effect, for all that remains to be produced [would still exist] due to the absence of parts; if it were possessed of parts, there would be a contradiction with the scriptures that proclaim its current lack of parts. Therefore, its status as a cause is refuted in both ways; this [objection] too has its essence extracted, because of its distinct nature, because it is thus made known by the scriptures through various modes, and because it possesses causal power.
No fruit whatsoever is observed from the attainment of desires; nor is this creation [brought about] by the Supreme out of compassion, since it is the sole cause of suffering.

He does not create this merely for sport, but rather under the influence of the necessity of merit and so forth. There is no partiality and the like, because the dependence on karma is established by its beginninglessness.

Because of the contradiction with the Smṛti of Kapila, because of the contradiction with the Smṛti of Hiraṇyagarbha, because of the contradiction with logic, because of the consequence of [continued] experience, and because of the difference between the effect and the cause. || 11 ||
Because of the identity of the individual soul and Brahman, because of the abandonment of the collection of causal factors,
because of the state where only the effect remains, and because of the disappearance of the fruit, [the Lord] removed that which had arisen.
By two [reasons] there would be no contradiction with the Smṛti; by the remaining ones, there is no contradiction with logic.
Among those, the fourth and fifth [reasons] are mentioned incidentally along with what was stated in the third.
Therefore, in this verse, when it is considered as a coherent whole, the sixth and the third [syllables] are joined;
indeed, four syllables beginning with the sixth join together in their proper sequence. (13)
"Arising through words that reflect its shadow, and likewise emergence through logic"—thus there would be a most beautiful connection with the preceding quarter-verse. (14)
The second quarter [of the verse]:

Although the number of principles (tattva-saṃkhyā) brought forth by the Vedas and the Tantra both desire many individual souls (jīva-s), that [Vedic number] indeed depends upon the agent (kartṛ), whereas this Tantric one does not; therefore, it is not incorrect. 15.
Even if there were a Lord as the creator and many individual souls (jīvas), nevertheless, a logical conclusion is not possible;
for, due to their being partless atoms, they lack the means to produce an effect, and because they are effects themselves, they possess no form [of agency]. (16)
"Indeed, for the atoms of the Saṃghas, there would be earth and so forth, and from the elements such as earth, there would be instruments and so forth.
This too is insubstantial; since all things are momentary, where could they possibly aggregate, and where could the accomplishment of an effect take place? (17)
If it is argued that "there is only one aspect [of cognition] because there is no dispute regarding cognition;

therefore, the object does not exist," this too is incorrect, because there is the manifestation of a triad: the cognition, the object of cognition, and its support, just as in the case of consciousness itself.

Because it would follow that [the world] arises eternally, an unmodified existence is not at all possible; nor does a modified existence possess logical consistency, since it would entail the loss of its established state.

Therefore, the world being produced from nothingness could not belong to any real entity (*sad-vastu*); for if such a distinction between existence and non-existence were applied to anything other than that [reality], the status of "nothingness" (*tucchatva*) would be lost. (19)

Furthermore, the claim that "all things, such as sentient beings and so forth, are distinct when existing as cloth and the like, yet non-distinct, stable and unstable"—this too is incorrect, because two contradictory properties cannot have a single substratum, and thus no cognition could be produced by anything else [to establish such a thing]. (20)

The view that the Lord of Beasts is worthy of respect because of his omniscience and his being the Supreme Lord is also incorrect, due to his teaching of doctrines contrary to the Vedas regarding the nature of dharma and the higher and lower principles. || 21 ||

"Because it is seen to contradict the Vedas through such statements as 'the individual soul [arises] from the Supreme' and 'the mind [arises] from the individual soul,' the Pañcarātra would not be true"—this argument is baseless, because [the Pañcarātra] teaches the manifestation of the Vyūhas and because it refutes [such a view]. || 22 ||
Kapila, Kaṇabhuj, and the Buddhas, along with Arhats and Śambhu, have been struck down by these arguments sharpened by the thunderbolt—arguments for which they possessed no harsh intellect.
Furthermore, it has been established that this path of the venerable Pañcarātra, as seen by the Blessed One, is indeed not at all similar to other external systems. || 23 ||
Having established the non-contradiction with tradition and logic, as well as the refutation of opposing views,
the nature of the effect is then considered in the following two verses.
The third quarter [of the verse]:

"Just as living beings possess origination, so too the ether does not possess origination because of the loss of its parts"—if the Śruti speaks thus, it would indeed be so; however, this does not constitute a refutation of reasoning (tarka). || 25 ||
All effects arise from their respective causes through other locations, as is heard [in scripture];
they do not, however, arise beyond those various bodies in this manner, because scripture shows no such intervention. || 26 ||
Because of the sense of the statement, "by means of the toy [he creates] living beings," the soul (jīva) is indeed born according to the proposition;

however, this is without merit, because it would entail the fallacy of the destruction of what has been done (kṛtavipraṇāśa) and because of the scriptural testimony that "[the soul] is eternal. || 27 ||
Because consciousness is not perceived during sleep, [one might argue that] cognition is adventitious or that the conscious being is distinct [from the Self].

This is not so, because of the scriptural testimony; the designation "knowledge" in deep sleep must be understood as restricted [to the waking state], since [the Self] is characterized by that quality [of knowledge] as its essence.
It should not be suspected that in such passages as "not other than the qualities" (nānyaṃ guṇebhyaḥ) his agency is being denied, whereby he would therefore not be the agent;
for this is not to be so doubted, because the meaning of the scripture is thus established and because it is logically consistent. || 29 ||
His agency is independent of anything else, for this is necessary so that the scriptures may have purpose; he is indeed autonomous.
This is not contradicted by the Śrutis, nor is there any conflict with the scriptures, because the Supreme Being depends upon [the soul's] effort.
Because of the difference [between them], there is indeed a mutual contradiction among the Śruti texts that the individual soul (jīva) is not a part [of Brahman].
However, because the Smṛti speaks of the soul as a part and because it is taught as being like a foot [of Brahman], the individual soul must indeed be a part of that Supreme Being.
The status of being an effect belongs to ether and the other elements, as does their lack of interval [from Brahman];
the absence of birth belongs to the individual soul (jīva), as do its nature as knower and its nature as agent. (32)
The dependence of agency upon another, as well as the state of being a constituent part in relation to another—all these matters have been considered in this verse. (33)
The first, second, and third [chapters] are connected here;
the remaining four chapters of the third [section], however, are considered here by way of incidental discussion.
The fourth quarter [of the verse] states: For there is no production of the senses, because of the scriptural text, "The vital breaths (prāṇāḥ) came into being first.
It is not so; rather, the vital breath (prāṇa) is supreme according to the formal proposition, and the plural number is merely figurative. 35.
[The opponent argues: "But from the statement 'seven indeed' and also from the Śruti text 'there are seven prāṇas,' [the number must be seven].
[We reply: Not so, because of their subordinate status; for from the statement "these ten," as well as from Smṛti, [it is established that there are ten]. (36)
It is indeed appropriate that those [breaths] are manifold, because of the scriptural statement, "All are infinite and equal.
It is not so, however, because they serve the purpose of meditation (*upāsti*), and because of the scriptural texts concerning departure (*utkramaṇa*) regarding their departure. || 37 ||
On account of the scriptural statement and common usage, this [prāṇa] is suspected to be neither mere air nor its function;
rather, it is the air that sustains the body and so forth, because of the distinct terminology used for "prāṇa" and "air" in the scriptural passages.
One should not entertain the doubt that the Lord (Vibhu) could be the vital breath (prāṇa) because of the statement regarding His equality with the three worlds;
for the scriptural mention of His equality with the worlds through such terms as "departure" (utkrānti) and so forth is merely an arthavāda (explanatory praise).
In this context, the presiding over speech and the other organs would belong to the individual soul (jīva) by its own nature, along with the fire and the rest;
it is not so for the Supreme Self because of the meditation [on them] as those [organs], yet this is because of the scriptural statement, "He who is in the fire. (40)

Because it is designated as a *prāṇa* and because its function is similar [to that of the other senses], this [nose] might clearly also be considered a sense organ (*indriya*), even though it is the most excellent (*śreṣṭha*).
This is not so, because of the designation "ten," and because the *prāṇa* and the *manas* are therefore also [not included among the sense organs]. (41)
The creation of names and so forth proceeds from Hiraṇyagarbha, because of the statement "by this [name]";
it is not thus from the Supreme Being alone, for that [creation] has as its common agent the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) performed through His body. (42)
The origin, enumeration, and measurement of the organs;
as well as the essential nature, measurement, and non-sensory character of the vital breath (prāṇa). || 43 ||
"He is the creator of all these individual manifestations"—
thus has this entire matter been correctly reflected upon by means of this quarter-verse.

In the first [section], all five types have been considered as they occur; in the second and subsequent sections, they are likewise. Therefore, both the first and the last [types] are appropriately included in this chapter.
The contemplation on the nature of the vital breath (prāṇa) is established incidentally through the mention of it as the vital breath of the organs;
and from that incidental context follows the contemplation on its specific characteristics. || 46 ||
The creation of those things situated outside the egg has been contemplated by the former [method];
however, the creation of those existing within the egg should be contemplated by this [method] as well. || 47 ||
The first position:
The embodied soul does not go accompanied by the subtle elements, precisely because those [elements] are easily available [elsewhere].
This is not so; for it departs together with them, since the Śruti declares, "The waters become persons. (1)
By these very statements beginning with "having reached the end," it follows that the individual soul (jīva) arrives [there] and is not one who possesses residual karma;
for this fruit is not dependent on karma, as it is heard in scripture [to apply even to those] "of evil conduct. || 2 ||

Because of the non-specific term "whosoever they may be," it might be thought that smoke and so forth [are the destination] for mere sinners; however, this would be incorrect, because the specific term "those who" (in the phrase "atha ye") refers to those who rely upon merit. || 3 ||
The state of having that body would be a condition of ether and so forth, since there is no distinction [from that] as there is in the case of being the moon;
this is not so, because there is no experience here [in ether etc.], therefore in this case there is only similarity, not the actual nature of that body.
This [process] concludes either quickly or after a long time because of the absence of a fixed rule regarding the state of being unhusked;
however, one should not suspect this to be so, because of the subsequent distinction made in the statement, "For from that, it is difficult to emerge. || 5 ||
Because of the specific term "are born," living beings indeed possess bodies such as rice and so forth.
This designation of "birth" is not figurative, because there is no reason for it to be so, and because [the state of being] exists subsequently.
Embracing by means of subtle elements, being accompanied by the remainder of karma, not ascending among the meritorious, and resembling the ether and other [subtle elements]. (7)
In this regard, the non-durable state of rice and other grains, as well as their coagulation—these six meanings have been correctly considered by means of this verse. (8)
The contemplation on the manner of going and coming is undertaken with the desire to serve for the sake of attaining renown;
yet, if one does not perceive even the slightest fault residing within oneself, then indeed one worships the Supreme.

It should not be suspected that the individual soul (jīva) is the creator of dream-objects on account of its possession of qualities (guṇitva) and its proximity (sannidhi); for such harmful activity is impossible, both because the soul is concealed (tirohita) and because its [true] quality is obscured.
In the Śruti, because no distinction is perceived, the state of deep sleep might be in the channels (nāḍīs), the pericardium (purītat), or the Supreme (Brahman).
But this is not so regarding the "ground" (bhūmi), because that would involve the fault of optionality (vikalpa), as in the case of sleeping on a palace, a couch, or a bed. || 11 ||
Because all karma is destroyed through the attainment [of the Self], the other [state] is the awakened one and not the deep sleeper;
for there would otherwise be no purpose for injunctions and rituals, and because of the recollection [of the dreamer] and the Vedic text, "Like a tiger. (12)
Fainting is indeed death due to the withdrawal of all the senses and the cessation of their functions;
yet in one who is fainting, there is a partial attainment of death, as evidenced by the irregularity of physical form and the restoration of consciousness. (13)
Or, because it is utterly to be abandoned by one's own will, contact with pus and the like is the fault of another;
[this is not so] because of the statement regarding the quality of being entirely free from defects in all cases. 14.

If it is argued that transformation [of Brahman] into the state of non-consciousness (acetana) is refuted by the reasoning of its being both manifold and one, then there would be a contradiction with the scripture stating its faultlessness; or if it is argued that there is a connection with a single commonality between those two, this cannot be, for nowhere in the world is a "bald man" ever referred to by the word "fragmented. Therefore, the state of being a part and the state of being the whole must belong to both the world and Brahman, just as they do to the self. || 15 ||

That there is some other goal to be attained even beyond that [Brahman] is not so, because it is designated as a bridge, because it is described as being limited, because of the scriptural statement of reaching it, and because of the apprehension of a distinction in the words, "That which is higher than that. This is because [Brahman] is indivisible, because it is the object of meditation, and because it is designated as the cause by virtue of being the means to liberation. || 16 ||

Since it is observed that [an action] yields fruit either directly or through a sequence, let karma itself bestow the fruit here as well; however, because this [karma] is cast away for the sake of another purpose, it is that [Supreme Being] alone who grants it, according to both Śruti and Smṛti.
Dreaming, deep sleep, awakening, and fainting belong to the individual soul (jīva) as well as to the Supreme (para).
[The attributes of the Supreme are] the state of being free from defects, the state of being a part of the universe, universal sovereignty, and the quality of being the bestower of fruits. || 18 ||
The remainder of the first chapter has been reflected upon by means of the four initial principles;
therefore, in this chapter, [the discussion] beginning from the fifth [section] is well-integrated.

Because it is the locus, because of its identity with the non-conscious, because of its inferiority, and because it does not bestow fruits—this doubt that [Brahman] is not to be worshipped is shattered here by the four subsequent [verses]. 20.
The knowledge is distinct because it is heard without qualification and because there is a difference in context; [the opponent replies:
"Not so, because the practitioners are distinct and because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth. (21)
The identity of the *udgītha* [meditation] for the Chandogas and the Vājasaneyins is not established on the grounds of the non-difference of the injunctions and so forth;
for there is no identity of form between the *udgītha* as a part of the rite and the *udgītha* as the object of meditation upon Prāṇa, and the same applies to the ritual action and its agent. (22)
Although the preeminence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth exists, its status as the "most excellent" (*vasiṣṭhatā*) and other qualities were not mentioned;
for there is no distinction [between them] due to a difference in form, since they are non-different from that which is other than them. (23)
Because they are not mentioned in the specific context [of the individual Upaniṣads], qualities such as bliss (ānanda) and the rest are not to be included.
However, it cannot be argued that [these qualities apply] to all [Upaniṣads], for without them, those [texts] cannot be defined. || 24 ||
The act of sipping water (*ācamana*) enjoined by the command "one should sip water" is a different *ācamana* that serves as an ancillary to the meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

This [sipping] is not merely restated here as something to be enjoined, because the state of being clothed by the vital breath (*prāṇavāsastva*) has not been previously established [as a requirement]. (25)

Because it is distinguished by the excellence of the power over truth through resolve and so forth, there is indeed no difference between this [power] and the various forms [of mastery], since the power of mastery is simply the expansion of the truth of resolve. (26)
Because there is no difference between the two objects of worship—the radiant one (the Sun) and the one seated on the senses (the Self)—there are two [deities] called by both names.
They are not distinct due to a difference in form; rather, they are established under a single name according to their respective locations. || 27 ||

Because it is stated without reference to anything specific, the "supporting of heroic powers" (saṃbhṛti-vīryāṇām) extends to all [the stages]; however, this is not so because the "pervasion of heaven" (dyu-vyāpti) cannot be grasped as occupying only a small portion. 28.
There is a distinction between the two knowledges despite the identity of their name as "Puruṣavidyā.
The mantras beginning with "śaṃ no mitre," being recited in proximity [to the main rite], are auxiliary parts of that knowledge;
for they are not auxiliary parts of the study [of the Veda] like the Śukra-mantras and others, precisely because of their functional capacity (sāmarthya). || 30 ||

In this context, either the loss and acquisition of merit and so forth should be considered as a single [process], or they should be considered as combined; for they are taught separately as distinct results. This is not the case because of mutual dependence upon one another. (31)
One should consider the loss of merit and so forth during the journey, at the time of death, and on the path;
however, such concern must never be entertained regarding death itself, as it has been stated that "for that long [one remains]. || 32 ||
The consideration of the path beginning with light (arcis) as taught in that [Vaiśvānaravidyā] would apply to those established in that very knowledge;
however, this is not so because of the difference in context, whereas the statement "those who... indicates equality.
The qualities beginning with "not gross" (asthūla) and so forth, which are taught as specific to [the knowledge of] Brahman, apply only there;

they do not apply elsewhere, because that would result in a loss of their status as valid measures of reality, nor because they function as qualifiers in the same manner as bliss (ānanda) and other such attributes. || 34 ||
Likewise, there is a difference between the two questioners, as well as an exchange regarding the destruction of life and so forth;
yet the statement "that which is directly," being common to both questions, is like the knowledge of Being (sadvidyā). || 35 ||

If the two [meditations] resting on the ether were not to be worshipped together as one *dahara-vidyā*, it would be because of the commonality of their qualities; for in some instances, the term "ether" signifies the heart. (36)

The meditation on the *udgītha* would be obligatory, like [the meditation on] the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), because it rests upon them; however, there is no such obligation because [the meditation] has its own purpose and because even one who does not perform the meditation remains a performer of the ritual action. (37)
Because of the reason of commonality, however, the possessor of qualities (guṇin) does not need to be repeated in the considerations of the qualities;
it is not so, because of the distinction [of each quality], for the possessor of qualities must indeed be repeated for every individual quality. (38)

It is not the case that the determination of the object of meditation for the "Dahara" (small) meditation follows the method of the preceding section simply because it is the subject at hand; rather, the determination of the whole [subject] is made on the strength of its own specific scriptural context. || 39 ||

Since the fires consisting of bricks and so forth are not subject to one's own injunction regarding their ritual performance, they must be understood as consisting of knowledge (vidyāmaya) because an injunction is to be inferred from the scriptural statement; thus, the fires such as "mind-made" (manaścita) and others are composed of knowledge.
The individual soul (jīva), characterized by agency and so forth, is the object of meditation because it possesses a body;

however, [the Supreme Self] endowed with the eightfold qualities is not [the object of meditation] in this way, because it is that which is to be attained, according to the principle of "as one intends, so one becomes" (yathākratu-nyāya). || 41 ||

It should not be suspected that the meditation on the *udgītha* is restricted solely to its own respective [Vedic branches] and not others, because there is no such limitation; for meditation has as its object the *udgītha* alone, regardless of the branch. (42)
In both cases, because of the connection with the fruit, Vaiśvānara is to be meditated upon either individually or collectively;
nor indeed can he be only the collective one, because of the prohibition [of such a view]. || 43 ||
The knowledges such as "Being" (sad-vidyā) would be one because there is no difference in their injunctions regarding the fruit and so forth;
yet this is not so, for they must indeed be distinct due to the differences in their names and forms. (44)
The various vidyās, such as the Sadvidyā and others, may involve a greater degree of dependence on the experience of Brahman;
however, there is no combination [of these vidyās] in a single instance, because the fruit is identical in every respect.
However, the absence of a rule for the meditative reflection on the *udgītha* and so forth was not stated previously;
for [meditation] lacks fruit in its own context, whereas in this case, there is a fruitful injunction regarding the locus [of meditation]. (46)

The identity of the knowledge, the distinction regarding the *udgītha*, the unity of the meditation on *prāṇa*, the collection of [qualities] such as bliss, and the injunction concerning the dwelling in *prāṇa*. (47)

The identity of Śāṇḍilya, the regulation of the two names, the pervasiveness of the sky, the distinction of the meditation on the Person, and its status as a subsidiary to the study of the Vedas and so forth. (48)

The mutual relationship between decrease and so forth is time, because of the injunction for reflecting upon it; likewise, there is commonality with the path of recollection and similarity with that which is not gross and so on. (49)
The unity of the vital breaths with hunger and so forth, and consequently the unity of the small space (dahara);
the lack of restriction regarding the meditation on the Udgītha, and the contemplation of the repetition of the qualities. || 50 ||

The definitive determination of all objects of worship, the status of the *manaściti*s as forms of knowledge (*vidyā*), the meditation on the individual soul (*jīva*) as possessing qualities, and the contemplation of the *udgītha* everywhere [are discussed]. (51)

The totality of Vaiśvānara, the distinctness of the knowledge of Being (sad-vidyā) and so forth, the non-aggregation of various knowledges, and furthermore, the lack of restriction regarding the Udgītha. || 52 ||
The distinction and non-distinction of the sciences, as well as the grasping and non-grasping of the qualities—thus has this been most excellently investigated by means of this quarter-verse. (53)
Because it is a subordinate part of the ritual action, the knowledge that determines the agent bestows the fruits upon that action;
it is not so for the Lord of the Jīva, because He is the determiner [of the soul], and the action is merely a subordinate part of His knowledge. (54)
Since only a connection with the *udgītha* and other parts of the ritual action is observed, the status of the *rasa* (essence) and so forth as praise is established;

therefore, a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*) cannot be inferred here on the grounds of proximity, the excellence of that which is already enjoined, or because it is not [otherwise] unestablished. || 55 ||
But names such as Pratardana and others are for the purpose of the *pāriplava* recitation due to their specific application;

however, names such as Manu and others serve the purpose of enjoining knowledge because they form a single syntactical unit with that [injunction] and because their own purposes have already been fulfilled.
But [it may be argued that] the knowledges (*vidyās*) are not possible for wandering mendicants (*pravrājakas*) because of the abandonment of sacrifices and their constituent parts.
This is not so; for since it is stated in scripture, "desiring which," that knowledge exists as being entirely independent of the sacrificial fires and other such requirements. (57)
Because householders share [the same duties] as those who have gone forth, that [knowledge] is deficient in its constituent parts for them;

however, it is not so with sacrifices and the like, because of the existence of scriptural injunctions and because [these duties] exist everywhere as the specific dharmas of one's own stage of life (āśrama). || 58 ||
Because they are appointed to active duties, their knowledge is not endowed with tranquility and the like.
This is not so, however, because tranquility and the rest are auxiliary members (*aṅga*) to that [knowledge], since the two have different bases. || 59 ||
The rule that those who know the vital breath (prāṇa) may eat all kinds of food at all times due to the absence of specific restrictions is not tenable;
for we observe that even a knower of Brahman who possesses special powers does not do so when his life is in danger.

Sacrifices and other rites belonging to the stages of life (*āśrama*) are not devoid of knowledge, because there is no contradiction [between them]. How could there be a constant result from that which is other than those? This contingency does not arise, because of the difference in application (*viniyoga*).
The qualification for knowledge does not belong to those outside the stages of life (anāśramins) because of their abandonment of the collection of constituent parts of rituals such as sacrifice;
this is not so, however, because it is observed in the case of Raikva and others, and because of the assistance provided by practices such as recitation and fasting.
The qualification for [the practice of] Vidyā does not belong to those who have fallen away from it due to their lack of approval for practices such as recitation (japa) and fasting (upavāsa).
This is because of the Smṛti, because of the observation that there is a loss when those [practices] are abandoned, and because of their exclusion by the learned (śiṣṭa).
That meditation which is connected with the constituent parts of a ritual belongs to its master, because he is the enjoyer of its fruit.
An animal, however, cannot possess that [meditation] as a constituent part of the ritual, for the very reason that it is connected with the constituent parts of the ritual. (64)
Because it is for the purpose of enjoining "one must reflect," the term "silence" (mauna) is restated; otherwise, it would be incorrect.
For in common worldly usage, "silence" is well known as referring to excellent reflection; therefore, this [quality] is what is to be enjoined. || 65 ||
For the wise one, however, there is the abandonment of what is to be performed; thus, "childhood" refers to all such things as the practice of desires, and this [is not for him].
Specifically, according to statements such as "not for those who have not ceased [from evil]," "childhood" means the non-manifestation of one's lineage and so forth. (66)
Sacrifices and the like, however, are causes for prosperity and so forth; they would yield immediate fruit because there is no delay in their causal operation.

That [immediate result] does not occur when it is obstructed by more powerful [karmas], yet it would occur [if unobstructed] because it is enjoined by the scriptural passage beginning with "That which... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10).
Ritual action performed for the sake of ultimate liberation would yield immediate fruit because of its inherent power;
yet even that does not apply to those foremost among the knowers of Brahman, because [for them] acts such as censure possess an exceedingly superior force.

The bestowal of fruits by knowledge, the subordination of the vital fluids (rasa) and so forth, the status of sacrifices as limbs of knowledge, and likewise the [status] of knowledge for those who have renounced; || 69 ||
For householders, there is the supervision of knowledge, sacrifices, and so forth;
their dependence on tranquility and other [virtues], and the regulation of food. (70)
Likewise, even householdership is a form of action; so too is ritual such as sacrifice.
There is qualification for those who are widowed, while for those who have fallen away from their vows, there is a lack thereof.

In the meditation on the components of the sacrifice, there is the duty of the officiating priests and the injunction for silence; "childhood," however, refers to his lack of ostentation regarding his power, learning, and noble birth. (72)
"By the statement, 'If there is an obstruction, there is delay in the actions aimed at heaven and liberation,' the synthesis of the procedural requirements (itikartavyatā) has been considered. (73)

Since knowledge is the means [to liberation] and that [means] ought to be performed only once, there would have to be a single realization; this is not so, because it is enjoined as a form of worship (*upāsanā*), for knowledge is [of the nature of] cognition (*jñapti*).
For the Supreme is indeed to be worshipped as distinct from oneself, since difference is established everywhere;
yet He is not to be worshipped as the Self with the thought "I am He," because of the scriptural word "Thou art That" and because of His being the very Self of that [individual]. || 2 ||

Likewise, it should not be suspected that the status of being an object of meditation is indistinguishable for the secondary symbols (pratīkas) as it is for the others, because names and so forth are to be meditated upon by means of the vision of the Supreme Self. || 3 ||
The view of the *udgītha* applied to the sun is indeed superior to that applied to the lowly [fire], for action alone is the bestower of fruit;
yet even that [action] does not bestow fruit in any other way than through the worship of Him (the Sun). || 4 ||
[Objection: "The rule 'while sitting' must apply to all activities because of the abandonment of [other] specific conditions. [Reply:

This would not be so, because there is no specific condition of one-pointedness [in other activities], and because that [meditation] belongs to one who is seated, according to the scriptural injunction on meditation (*dhyāna*). (5)
Precisely because it is accomplished through the meaning of the treatise, that [practice] must be performed on a single day;
for this cannot be completed "throughout one's life," according to both the word and the injunction regarding it.

However, because of the recollection of the words "not [experienced] without being eaten," there is indeed no non-clinging or destruction of sins; for that [knowledge] is solely intended to establish the fruition [of karma], and because of the scriptural hearing: "one who knows thus. It is not so. || 7 ||
Attachment and destruction do not at all apply to beneficial actions for the sake of attaining happiness;
however, because they are equally obstructive to liberation, they clearly do apply to one who desires liberation. (8)
For one who abandons all specific designations (vaiśeṣika-śabda), there indeed occurs both non-clinging and destruction;
however, this does not apply to that which has already begun its effect, because the specific designation [is used] in the sense of "as long as I am not liberated. 9.
Because of the scriptural teaching on the destruction of attachment, there is the non-performance of one's own stage-of-life duties;
yet this is certainly not the case, because of the word "sacrifice" and because of the power of generating knowledge. (10)

Because of the specific word "until I am liberated," the action being undertaken has liberation as its fruit; furthermore, this [action] extends until the fall of that body, for that scriptural passage has that very fruit as its scope. || 11 ||

Because it is worshipped as an effect repeatedly, even the "I" (the ego) is an object of worship; however, in the case of symbols (*pratīka*), the worship is otherwise, such as viewing the limbs [of the body] as the sun and so forth. (12)
The worship has sitting as its constituent part, and it is to be performed every day; furthermore, there is the non-attachment to and destruction of sin, as well as the increase of merit. (13)
By this quarter, it is established that the fruits of actions undertaken bear results, that the duties of the stages of life (āśramas) must be performed,
and that bondage has its limit in karma.
Because speech would lose its status as having the mind as its cause, there can be no dissolution of the function of speech into the mind;
for that [mind] and speech do not share the same state, both by virtue of the word "speech" and because of their mere connection. (15)
Prāṇa consists of water because of its connection with the nature of water, according to the Vedic scripture: "Prāṇa is composed of water.
However, the mind (citta) is not produced by the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); rather, since prāṇa is an effect of ether (nabhas), it is that [ether] itself.
"The vital breath (prāṇa) would become united with fire (tejas) because of the mention of hearing sound;
this [would be so] were it not for the mention of the departure of the living self (jīva) and so forth, whereas the mention of fire occurs later. (17)

But fire (tejas), because it is heard in scripture as "that [is] fire," is indeed merely that subtle element (tanmātra) in its form devoid of other things; it would not be so, however, when it has entered into the other elements, because of the scriptural statement regarding its being made tripartite (trivṛtkṛta) and because [otherwise] it would lack the capacity [to produce effects]. || 18 ||
This, however, is the destination for the ignorant; for the wise, there is attainment right here, as indicated by the word "attainment" (parāpti).
These two cannot be the case, because the same departure from the body applies to both; the other [passage] is merely an explanatory statement (arthavāda). || 19 ||
Because they would be purposeless due to the absence of enjoyment and so forth, these [elements] would [dissolve] according to their respective [orders], but not into the deity;
it should not be suspected that "they merge into them," because of the scriptural injunction: "The fire [merges] into the highest. || 20 ||
However, for those three, dissolution will eventually occur in another person because they have him as their own cause;
that was clearly stated by the predecessors through a single sentence, and it refers merely to their conjunction, since there is no contradiction [otherwise]. (21)
The restriction that [the soul departs] through other channels at the crown of the head is not due to subtlety; rather, the scriptural statement indicates the possibility [of such a departure].
Therefore, by the excellence of the power of knowledge and through the grace of the Supreme, the journey occurs in that very manner.
In the case of the night-time [sun], there is no fixed rule regarding the prevention of the following of rays;
nor is there such a rule for the following of beams, because heat is perceived even at midnight, since these [rays] indeed exist.
For one who dies during the day, there is indeed an approach to another [world], because dying at night is censured;
however, this [consequence] would not occur due to the destruction of the karma that binds, by the power of knowledge (vidyā), as the Śruti also declares.
Indeed, there is no liberation for one who dies during the southern course of the moon; for it is heard in scripture that such a person attains union with the Moon.
Yet that is not due to the excellence of their knowledge; rather, that scriptural statement concerns the sphere of the Moon as a place of rest. (25)
Speech [is merged] in the mind; that [mind] in the vital breath; that again in the living soul and the mind (or the two heats);
the heat [is merged] through contact with the other; there is equality of that which consists of only so much. || 26 ||
Their departure to the next world, the mere nature of that [departure] as a connection, the regulation of the cranial channel, and the [path of the] ray—such is the established doctrine. (27)
And even at night there is liberation, as well as deliverance during the southern course;
all this has been contemplated here by means of this quarter-verse. (28)
The third quarter [of the verse]:
Because there is a variety of descriptions in the various branches [of the Upanishads], there is no restriction [to the path] beginning with light based on the scriptural mention of "going.
That restriction does not indeed apply, because signs such as the sun and so forth are possible everywhere. (29)
Furthermore, wind and the world of the gods would become distinct due to a difference in their sounds;
[otherwise] there would not be [the designation], "That which blows is the world of the gods," because of that qualification. || 30 ||
Even though the sequence of the Vedic revelation is broken, because there is no other way [to interpret it], Varuṇa and the others follow after Vāyu according to the textual reading;
however, by virtue of the sense of the matter, Varuṇa should be above Taṭit, and Indra and the others are above that. || 31 ||
Because the instruction is of that nature, the signs such as light (arciḥ) and so on belong to the path;
this is not so because of the word "conductor" (gamayitṛ), for even those beyond [the path] may be conducting deities (ātivāhika). || 32 ||

This is the goal for one who worships the Four-faced [Brahmā], for he is attained through the constant realization of the Supreme in its full perfection. That [attainment] is not for one who worships that which is beyond him; for according to scripture, that which is beyond is non-existent, as is seen from the scriptural evidence regarding both [the individual soul and the Supreme] in relation to life.
But there is a fixed order starting from the flame; the oneness of Vāyu and Svarga;
the reaching of Varuṇa from lightning; and from that, the state of being a guide (ātivāhika). || 34 ||
"The fruit of the worship of the individual soul and the Supreme, as well as this path beginning with light—everything has been considered by this very quarter [of the verse]. (35)

Furthermore, it would be incorrect to say that the liberated one has a connection with anything whatsoever—even with happiness—either in its own nature or in any other form, because [happiness] is always perceived as being devoid of bliss; moreover, this would contradict the word "by himself" (svena), since [the self] is not concealed. || 36 ||
The experience of another would occur through differentiation, whether by the word "similarity" (sādharmya) or the word "extreme similarity" (atisāmya).
This [experience] could not exist [in the sense of identity], because it consists of that [other]; thus, the mention of "similarity" depends upon the equality of their qualities. (37)

The nature of the liberated one consists of the eight qualities, because it is so heard in scripture; or else, it consists of mere radiance, because of the term "mass of consciousness" applied to that very same state. Therefore, both [views] may be true, as there is no contradiction between them. || 38 ||

The claim that for one who is liberated, parents and so forth will appear through effort and volition, as is observed in the case of Brahmā and others, is incorrect; for these [beings] lack the quality of having volitions that are inherently true. || 39 ||
The liberated one is bodiless because of the word "bodiless," yet possesses a body at will because of the word "in many ways.
This restriction [of being always bodiless] does not hold; rather, due to the word "in many ways" and the abundance of scriptural testimony, this [assumption of a body] must be voluntary. || 40 ||
Indeed, from the word "equality" (sāmya), the experience of one who is liberated would likewise imply the state of being the sustainer of the world;
this is not so for the Supreme [Lord] because of the word "thusness" (tathātva), for His experience is an enjoyment characterized by attributes (saguṇa). || 41 ||
The manifestation of one's own essential nature, the state of being the form of supreme experience, the discernment of the liberated self-nature, and likewise the power of true resolve; || 42 ||
"Enjoyment of all things according to one's own will, and the arising of the fruit of liberation"—this collection of meanings is what is intended by this quarter-verse. (43)
